paragraphs.heading: What counts as a storm
paragraphs.text: The word storm covers any disturbed state, whether of the natural environment or of the atmosphere of an astronomical body. It may show up as strong wind, hail, thunder and lightning, heavy rain or snow, heavy freezing rain, or wind carrying some substance through the atmosphere, as in a dust storm. The English word comes from the Proto-Germanic sturmaz, meaning "noise, tumult".

paragraphs.heading: How a storm forms
paragraphs.text: A storm forms when a center of low pressure develops and a system of high pressure surrounds it. Together these opposing forces can create winds and lead to storm clouds such as cumulonimbus. Small, local areas of low pressure can also form where hot air rises off hot ground. These produce smaller disturbances such as dust devils and whirlwinds.

paragraphs.heading: Harm and help
paragraphs.text: Storms can harm lives and property through storm surge, flooding from heavy rain or snow, impassable roads, lightning, wildfires and wind shear. Systems with significant rainfall and duration also help relieve drought in the places they pass through. Heavy snowfall can allow recreation that would not otherwise be possible, such as skiing and snowmobiling.

paragraphs.heading: Thunderstorms
paragraphs.text: A thunderstorm is a storm that produces both lightning and thunder, and it normally comes with heavy precipitation. Thunderstorms happen throughout the world. They are most frequent in tropical rainforest regions, where humidity and temperature are high and the atmosphere is unstable. They occur when high levels of condensation form in a body of unstable air that produces deep, rapid upward motion in the atmosphere.

paragraphs.heading: Ice storms
paragraphs.text: Ice storms are among the most dangerous kinds of winter storm. They can happen when the surface is colder than freezing while, higher up, a thick layer of air stays warmer than freezing. Rain can then fall into the freezing layer and freeze on impact into a glaze of ice. In general, 8 millimetres of ice is all it takes to start bringing down power lines and tree limbs, especially when it is breezy. Ice storms can last from hours to days.

paragraphs.heading: Snow and fire
paragraphs.text: A snowstorm is a heavy fall of snow that builds up at more than 5 centimeters per hour and lasts several hours. A blizzard, in general, comes with gale-force winds, heavy snow and very cold conditions, though its definition varies over time and by location. A firestorm is a fire so intense that it creates and sustains its own wind system. Most often it arises naturally, during some of the largest forest fires and wildfires.

paragraphs.heading: Storms over the ocean
paragraphs.text: Out at sea, storm conditions are defined as sustained winds of 48 knots (90 km/h) or more. Such a storm can sink vessels of every type and size. A bomb cyclone is the rapid deepening of a mid-latitude low-pressure area, typically over the ocean. The winds in these storms can be as powerful as those of a typhoon or hurricane.
